title: What you still don't know
hook: open questions are part of the path

segments.voice: Yesterday: the teachers you met. Your line was thank the teachers. Did you write your line: from this person, I learned this? Day three hundred twenty-nine.

Almost a year on this path. Stories, practices, seven traditions visited as a guest, weeks in the lab. So by now, surely, you have some answers. Is there a God? What happens when we die? What is the self that breathes? Which way of living is right for you? If you're honest, you may have fewer answers than when you started, and better questions. That can feel like failure. As if the point of a year like this was to arrive somewhere with everything settled. But some of the teachers we met would smile at that. Today: what you still don't know.
screen: `ALMOST A YEAR ON THE PATH.` → `FEWER ANSWERS, BETTER QUESTIONS.` → `THE OLD TEACHERS WOULD SMILE.`

segments.voice: First, Socrates. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury that his friend asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the oracle said no one was. He was baffled, so he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom. His conclusion: they thought they knew things they didn't. He, at least, didn't think he knew what he didn't know. That, he decided, was his small edge. We met him on day eighty-six, saying I don't know out loud. Second, learned ignorance. In 1440, the German churchman and philosopher Nicholas of Cusa, later a cardinal, wrote a book called On Learned Ignorance, docta ignorantia. His argument, from inside his Christian faith, was that the infinite can't be fully grasped by a finite mind, and that knowing the limits of your knowing is itself a kind of learning. Third, living the questions. The poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young poet who had sent him his questions. Be patient with what's unsolved in your heart, he advised; try to love the questions themselves; live them now, and perhaps someday you'll live your way into an answer. Fourth, why this matters on this path. The traditions offer answers, and people find real peace in them. This path doesn't hand you one, and it never will. It points to where the traditions keep their answers, and leaves the choosing to you. So an honest list of what you still don't know isn't a gap in the year. It's a map of where you're still alive and curious. Zhuangzi and his friend Huizi never settled whether anyone can know the joy of fish. The conversation was the point.
screen: `SOCRATES: NOT PRETENDING TO KNOW.` · `CUSA: LEARNED IGNORANCE.` · `RILKE: LOVE THE QUESTIONS.` · `A MAP OF WHERE YOU'RE CURIOUS.` · then, large: `STILL ASKING.`

segments.voice: Find the question you wrote six days ago, the one beyond the lab, and put it at the top of a page or a note. Add two more you still can't answer. Big or small. About God, death, yourself, a person in your life, how to live. Don't answer them. Read the three back slowly and notice which one pulls hardest. Let that one keep you company. The bell holds the time.
What you still don't know. The open questions you carry, not as failure, but as a map of where you're still curious. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT YOU STILL DON'T KNOW — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: still asking. Keep your three questions somewhere safe. Today, say I don't know once, out loud, when it's true. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Philosophers and many religious thinkers have treated honest not-knowing as part of wisdom; people on their own path often keep a short list of open questions and return to it over the years.
